title: Four, five times
hookLine: Uttama left her cell again and again, restless, until the day she stayed (Therigatha, Uttama)

cards: A door opens. A nun steps out of her small dwelling and stands there. She can't settle.
She goes back in and sits. Before long she's on her feet and out again. The Therigatha doesn't hide this, and neither does she.
In her own poem a nun named Uttama counts it: four times, five times, she went out of her dwelling, with no peace of mind and her thoughts out of her control. It's an honest number. Not once.

teach.b: First, the leaving. Uttama had gone forth. She had a place to sit, and she kept getting up.
The restlessness wasn't something she'd outgrown before she joined; it came with her into the robe. Second, the help.

Then, the poem says, she went to a nun she could trust, who taught her the dhamma: how a person is made of changing parts, the senses and their objects, the elements. She didn't solve her restlessness alone in her room.
She went and asked someone. Third, the sitting. Having heard the teaching, she did what she'd been taught, and the poem says she sat in one posture for seven days, steeped in joy and ease.
Fourth, the darkness broken. On the eighth day she stretched out her legs, having torn through the mass of darkness, the same picture as Punna's poem: wisdom breaking the dark.
So the shape of Uttama's poem is out, out, out, then help, then stillness. The four and five times aren't cut from the story to make her look better.
They're the first line. The tradition kept the count of her leavings right beside the moment she came free, as if the leaving were part of the path that led to the staying.
And the staying came after the help, not instead of the leaving.

how: Some meditation teachers describe noticing the wandering mind and returning to the breath as the heart of sitting practice, and Uttama's verse is read as an honest account of restlessness on the way to stillness.

o: the nuns who taught Uttama the dhamma
how often Uttama left before she stayed
the days Uttama sat without moving

s: Uttama found peace the first time she sat down
four times, five times, she went out of her dwelling without peace.
Uttama went to another nun for help
a nun she could trust taught her the dhamma, and then she sat.
the poem leaves out her restlessness
the restlessness is the poem's first line.

games.q: you're Uttama. four, five times you've left your dwelling, restless, your thoughts out of control. what do you do next?
o: give up the robe and go home.
go to a nun you trust and listen.
lock yourself in and try harder alone.
games.why: she goes to a nun she trusts, hears the teaching, and then sits in one posture until the darkness breaks.

practice: Sit with the breath, on a cushion or a chair. The mind may leave four times, five times, more; each time you see it has gone, come back, and don't count the leaving as failure. Out, and back: the coming back is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Four. Four times, five times, Uttama left her dwelling without peace, until, with help, she sat and stayed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali catukkhattuṃ: four times. The opening word of Uttama's verse.

carryVoice: Your line: she stayed. Four, five times out, and then the time she stayed. That's day seven hundred eighty-five.

sources.ref: Therigatha commentary on Uttama (the teacher named as Patacara)
